items.title: Buddhism rejects the existence of a permanent self
items.claim: What is the Buddhist teaching of anatta?

options.text: The soul is eternal and unchanging
There is no permanent, unchanging self (atman); what we call 'self' is a constantly changing aggregation of five skandhas (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness)
Only the body is real; the soul is illusion

items.reveal:
Anatta (no-self) is one of the three marks of existence in Buddhism, alongside anicca (impermanence) and dukkha (unsatisfactoriness). The doctrine sharply distinguishes Buddhism from Hinduism's atman/Brahman teaching.

The Anattalakkhana Sutta — the Buddha's second sermon — argues each of the five skandhas is impermanent and not under our control, so cannot be 'self'.

Later Mahayana schools developed the concept further. Yogacara introduced 'alaya-vijnana' (storehouse consciousness); some Pure Land traditions speak of 'Buddha-nature' that complicates the picture without abandoning anatta.
items.why: Anatta is one of the most counter-intuitive religious doctrines. It contradicts both Western theological assumptions about the soul and lived experience of continuity — and is the central philosophical claim of Buddhism.

items.title: Jihad means 'struggle' — and has a greater inner meaning
items.claim: What is the classical Islamic distinction between greater and lesser jihad?

options.text: Greater jihad is large-scale war; lesser jihad is small skirmishes

A widely cited hadith distinguishes the 'lesser jihad' (armed struggle in defence of the community) from the 'greater jihad' (the inner struggle against one's own ego) — though the hadith's authenticity is debated by some scholars
Jihad means only armed warfare; it has no inner meaning
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Scholars including Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and modern critics question the hadith's authenticity. But the inner-struggle understanding is found independently in Sufi traditions and in mainstream piety.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: Act and rule utilitarianism give different answers
items.claim: What is the distinction between act and rule utilitarianism?

options.text: They are alternative names for the same theory

Act utilitarianism judges each action by its consequences directly; rule utilitarianism asks which rules, if generally followed, would produce the greatest happiness — and applies those rules even when an individual act might seem to maximise utility differently
Act utilitarianism is the only legitimate form

items.reveal:
Jeremy Bentham's 'Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789) introduced the hedonic calculus. John Stuart Mill's 'Utilitarianism' (1861) distinguished higher and lower pleasures.

Rule utilitarianism (developed by R.M. Hare and Richard Brandt in the 20th century) attempts to address objections to act utilitarianism — that it permits horrific acts (killing one innocent to save five) and creates impossible decision burdens.

Critics argue rule utilitarianism collapses into act utilitarianism (just add 'except in special cases') or into Kantian deontology (just follow the rules).
items.why: Utilitarianism is not one theory. The act/rule distinction changes the answers radically — and exam answers that treat 'utilitarianism' as monolithic miss the most important internal debate.
